title: Finite coactions and colinear maps descend along a directed coalgebra limit
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $I$ be a nonempty set with a directed preorder, so any two indices have a common upper bound. For each $i\in I$ let $D_i$ be a $k$-vector space with linear maps $\Delta_i:D_i\to D_i\otimes_kD_i$ and $\epsilon_i:D_i\to k$ satisfying $(\Delta_i\otimes1)\Delta_i=(1\otimes\Delta_i)\Delta_i$ and $(\epsilon_i\otimes1)\Delta_i=(1\otimes\epsilon_i)\Delta_i=1_{D_i}$. Use tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Suppose $u_{ij}:D_i\to D_j$ for $i\leq j$ are linear maps preserving $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$, with $u_{ii}=1$ and $u_{j\ell}u_{ij}=u_{i\ell}$. Let $(D,\iota_i)$ be the vector-space colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. There is a unique coalgebra structure on $D$ with $\Delta\iota_i=(\iota_i\otimes\iota_i)\Delta_i$ and $\epsilon\iota_i=\epsilon_i$.
For any finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $M$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] and right $D$-coaction $\rho:M\to M\otimes_kD$, meaning $(\rho\otimes1)\rho=(1\otimes\Delta)\rho$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\rho=1_M$, there are $i$ and a right $D_i$-coaction $\rho_i$ on the same $M$ such that $\rho=(1_M\otimes\iota_i)\rho_i$. Moreover, let $M,N$ be finite-dimensional right $D_i$-comodules and let $a:M\to N$ be $k$-linear. If $a$ is colinear after extension to $D$, there is $j\geq i$ for which $a$ is colinear for the $D_j$-coactions obtained by composing with $1\otimes u_{ij}$. Neither injectivity of the transition maps nor finite-dimensionality of the $D_i$ is required.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, details of its passage to the directed limit; agent-explicit finite coaction and morphism descent underlying that passage.

proof.text: The maps $d_i=(\iota_i\otimes\iota_i)\Delta_i:D_i\to D\otimes_kD$ form a cocone: for $i\le j$, $d_ju_{ij}=(\iota_ju_{ij}\otimes\iota_ju_{ij})\Delta_i=d_i$. The $\epsilon_i$ also form a cocone. The colimit universal property defines unique linear maps $\Delta:D\to D\otimes_kD$ and $\epsilon:D\to k$ with the required composites. After precomposing with $\iota_i$, the two coassociativity maps both equal $\iota_i^{\otimes3}(\Delta_i\otimes1)\Delta_i=\iota_i^{\otimes3}(1\otimes\Delta_i)\Delta_i$, and each counit composite equals $\iota_i$. Colimit uniqueness proves the coalgebra identities. All tensor rebracketings here are the maps $x\otimes(y\otimes z)\leftrightarrow(x\otimes y)\otimes z$ induced by the tensor universal property.

source.place: Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, directed-limit passage; agent supplies the finite-coefficient argument, using Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00D6 (lemma-directed-colimit), 00D7 (lemma-zero-directed-limit), 00DD (lemma-tensor-products-commute-with-limits).

proof.text:
Apply the tensor-colimit theorem with constant ring system $A_i=k$ and module systems $M_i=N_i=D_i$. Its hypotheses on underlying abelian colimits hold: the quotient construction of directed abelian-group colimits has scalar action $a[x_i]=[ax_i]$, well defined by eventual equality; compatible linear maps descend by $[x_i]\mapsto f_i(x_i)$, which is linear by this formula. Thus that construction is a vector-space colimit, and its unique colimit isomorphism to $D$ respects every leg. The constant ring colimit is $k$, since a compatible cocone on a nonempty directed constant diagram has all its legs equal. The cited theorem consequently identifies
$$\varinjlim_i(D_i\otimes_kD_i)\ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ D\otimes_kD,\qquad [x\otimes y]_i\longmapsto\iota_i(x)\otimes\iota_i(y).$$
These are module colimits as well, by the same scalar formula. Hence the module-elementwise lemma detects the vanishing of any element of $D_i\otimes_kD_i$ at a later stage. This is an application of the existing varying-ring theorem, not an assumption that $\iota_i\otimes\iota_i$ is injective.

source.place: Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, directed-limit passage; agent supplies the finite-coefficient argument, using Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00D6 (lemma-directed-colimit), 00D7 (lemma-zero-directed-limit), 00DD (lemma-tensor-products-commute-with-limits).

proof.text:
Choose a finite basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $M$: starting with its finite spanning family, delete a vector whenever it is a combination of the others; the remaining family is independent and still spans. For any vector space $W$, the tensor universal property gives mutually inverse maps $W^n\to M\otimes_kW$, $(w_a)\mapsto\sum_a e_a\otimes w_a$, and $M\otimes_kW\to W^n$, $e_a\otimes w\mapsto(\delta_{ab}w)_b$. In particular write uniquely
$$\rho(e_b)=\sum_a e_a\otimes c_{ab},\qquad c_{ab}\in D.$$
Expanding the two coaction identities and applying the coordinate maps just constructed gives
$$\Delta(c_{ab})=\sum_t c_{at}\otimes c_{tb},\qquad\epsilon(c_{ab})=\delta_{ab}.$$
For example, the coefficient of $e_a$ in $(\rho\otimes1)\rho(e_b)$ is $\sum_t c_{at}\otimes c_{tb}$, fixing the order of the two tensor factors.

source.place: Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, directed-limit passage; agent supplies the finite-coefficient argument, using Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00D6 (lemma-directed-colimit), 00D7 (lemma-zero-directed-limit), 00DD (lemma-tensor-products-commute-with-limits).

proof.text: Use the module-elementwise lemma to represent each of the finitely many $c_{ab}$ by an element of some $D_{i_{ab}}$. Repeatedly take common upper bounds of those indices to obtain $i$ and lifts $c^i_{ab}\in D_i$ with $\iota_i(c^i_{ab})=c_{ab}$. Define the linear map $\widetilde\rho_i(e_b)=\sum_a e_a\otimes c^i_{ab}$. Its extension is $\rho$, but it need not yet satisfy coassociativity. The counit equations already hold: $\epsilon_i(c^i_{ab})=\epsilon\iota_i(c^i_{ab})=\delta_{ab}$, an equality in the fixed field $k$. If $n=0$, take any $i\in I$; all the displayed families and equations are empty and the zero map is the required coaction.

source.place: Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, directed-limit passage; agent supplies the finite-coefficient argument, using Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00D6 (lemma-directed-colimit), 00D7 (lemma-zero-directed-limit), 00DD (lemma-tensor-products-commute-with-limits).

proof.text:
For each pair $(a,b)$ put
$$z_{ab}=\Delta_i(c^i_{ab})-\sum_t c^i_{at}\otimes c^i_{tb}\ \in D_i\otimes_kD_i.$$
Its image in $D\otimes_kD$ is zero by steps 1 and 3. Step 2 and the module-elementwise lemma therefore give an index $j_{ab}\ge i$ at which $(u_{i j_{ab}}\otimes u_{i j_{ab}})(z_{ab})=0$. Choose one $j$ above these finitely many indices and $i$. Put $c^j_{ab}=u_{ij}(c^i_{ab})$. Since $u_{ij}$ preserves comultiplication, the image of $z_{ab}$ at $j$ is exactly $\Delta_j(c^j_{ab})-\sum_t c^j_{at}\otimes c^j_{tb}$; it is zero because transition maps take zero to zero. Counits remain $\delta_{ab}$ since $\epsilon_ju_{ij}=\epsilon_i$. Define $\rho_j(e_b)=\sum_a e_a\otimes c^j_{ab}$. The same coordinate expansion as in step 3 proves both coaction identities for $\rho_j$, and $\iota_ju_{ij}=\iota_i$ proves $(1_M\otimes\iota_j)\rho_j=\rho$.

source.place: Theorem 9.37, printed p.178, directed-limit passage; agent supplies the finite-coefficient argument, using Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00D6 (lemma-directed-colimit), 00D7 (lemma-zero-directed-limit), 00DD (lemma-tensor-products-commute-with-limits).

proof.text:
For the morphism assertion, choose finite bases $(e_b)$ of $M$ and $(f_s)$ of $N$ by the deletion argument of step 3. Write the given $D_i$-coactions and linear map as
$$\rho_M(e_b)=\sum_t e_t\otimes c_{tb},\quad\rho_N(f_s)=\sum_r f_r\otimes d_{rs},\quad a(e_b)=\sum_s A_{sb}f_s,$$
with $c_{tb},d_{rs}\in D_i$ and $A_{sb}\in k$. The coefficient of $f_r$ in $\rho_Na(e_b)-(a\otimes1)\rho_M(e_b)$ is
$$w_{rb}=\sum_s A_{sb}d_{rs}-\sum_t A_{rt}c_{tb}\in D_i.$$
Colinearity after extension to $D$ says exactly $\iota_i(w_{rb})=0$. The module-elementwise lemma kills each of these finitely many elements at a later index. A common upper bound $j\ge i$ kills them all, and coordinate expansion gives colinearity at $j$. The pushed maps are indeed coactions: expanding their coassociativity equations applies $1\otimes u_{ij}\otimes u_{ij}$ to the original equations, and the counit equation applies $\epsilon_ju_{ij}=\epsilon_i$. If either basis is empty there are no $w_{rb}$ and one may take $j=i$. No step cancels a transition map; neither injectivity nor any dimension bound on $D_i$ was used.
